1.sense: Opens with the same declaration that opens the surah before it and the one two after it: everything in the heavens and everything on the earth glorifying Allah as a standing fact, not a command being issued. Four titles follow in a run, Sovereign and Pure paired first, then Mighty and Wise, kingship set beside holiness and power beside wisdom. The pairing sets the register for what follows, a King who sends a messenger to a people rather than a force with no bearing on them.

notes.t: Yusabbihu is present tense, describing an ongoing action rather than a past declaration; the root s-b-h is also the root of swimming and moving swiftly through a course, so the glorifying pictured is closer to motion than to speech.
Al-Malik, al-Quddus and al-Aziz appear together again, alongside other names, in the closing verses of Al-Hashr, describing Allah in the same cluster of kingship, holiness and might.

links.why: the surah immediately before opens with this exact sentence, word for word
the same string of titles, Sovereign and Pure among them, closes a passage in Al-Hashr

2.sense: Names the mission behind the glorifying just declared: a messenger raised up among the ummiyyin, those without a prior scripture of their own, and drawn from among them rather than sent from outside. The mission runs in a fixed order, reciting the verses first, then purifying, then teaching the Book and wisdom, instruction following recitation rather than the reverse. The closing clause states what stood before him, open error, not a flawed guidance but its absence.

notes.t: Al-ummiyyin, the unlettered, is read as the Arabs who held no revealed book of their own before this messenger, distinct from the People of the Book named elsewhere in the Qur'an.
The same three-stage sequence, reciting the verses, purifying, teaching the Book and wisdom, closes with the same clause about earlier open error in a passage about the believers in Al Imran.
The Prophet ﷺ is named al-nabi al-ummiyy, the unlettered prophet, in a passage of Al-A'raf describing him as the one written of in the Torah and the Gospel.

links.why: the same mission, in the same order, closing on the same clause about earlier error
the title al-nabi al-ummiyy given to the same messenger

3.sense: Extends the mission of the verse before to others not yet come, joined to the first audience by the same messenger without a break in the sentence. Who these others are is left open here rather than named. The verse closes on the same two titles that closed the first verse, tying the sending of the messenger, present and future, back to Allah's kingship over creation.

notes.t: Asked who these others were, the Prophet ﷺ placed his hand on Salman al-Farisi, a Persian Companion, and said that if faith were suspended at the Pleiades, men from among these people would still reach it.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of Tafsir, from Abu Hurairah

notes.t: Lamma, translated here as "not yet", carries an expectation of what has not happened rather than a flat negation, keeping the mission open past the first hearers rather than closed with them.

4.sense: Closes the opening unit by naming the sending of the messenger, and its reach to those still to come, as fadl, grace given rather than earned. Fadl appears twice in four words, once as the gift and once as an attribute of the giver, before the verse states it a third time as great. The mission just described is set down as a gift, not a claim any people can make on Allah.

notes.t: Fadl is surplus, more than what is owed; naming the same word twice binds the mission of the two verses before it to grace rather than to any standing the recipients hold.
The identical sentence, that is the bounty of Allah, He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is possessor of great bounty, closes a passage on scripture and prophethood in Al-Hadid.

links.why: the same closing sentence, word for word, ends a passage in Al-Hadid

5.sense: Turns to those entrusted with the Torah who then set it down, drawn as a donkey loaded with books, carrying a weight of writing it cannot read. The comparison lands on the failure to carry rather than on any failure to receive; the load sits on its back the whole time. The verse widens at the end from this one people to a general rule, that Allah does not guide a people who deal with themselves this way.

notes.t: Hamala is used twice for two different kinds of carrying, first hummilu, made to bear a duty, then yahmilu, a physical load on the back; the donkey is faulted for carrying without reading, not for any lack of understanding as such.

Exegetes read this either as addressed to the Jews of Madinah who held knowledge of the Prophet's description in the Torah and withheld it, or as a general description of anyone entrusted with revealed knowledge who does not act on it; both readings are carried in the classical commentaries.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, on this verse

links.why: a related animal comparison, a man given signs who sheds them, likened to a panting dog
a related charge against scholars of the Book, writing scripture by hand and selling it cheaply

6.sense: Puts a direct challenge in the Prophet's mouth, addressed by name to those who follow Judaism. If a claimed standing before Allah, closed to the rest of mankind, is genuine, then wishing for death should follow easily, since death is what carries a person on to the reward such a standing would guarantee. The test is built entirely on their own claim rather than on anything the Qur'an asserts about them.

notes.t: Za'amtum, "you claim", is a verb the Qur'an regularly uses for an assertion made without proof, framing what follows as their own statement rather than a settled fact.

The same test, wishing for death if the reward of the afterlife belongs to a claimant people alone, is set in Al-Baqarah, with the added statement that they will never wish for it, being the people most attached to life.

links.why: the same challenge, with the further claim that they will never actually wish for death

7.sense: Answers the challenge of the verse before it, before anyone has a chance to take it up. The refusal is put down to what their hands have sent ahead of them, past deeds rather than present fear, and the verse closes by naming Allah's knowledge of wrongdoers instead of repeating the charge itself.

notes.t: Qaddamat aydihim, what the hands have sent forward, is a standing figure in the Qur'an for deeds banked ahead of a person for the reckoning, the hand standing for the deed it performed.
The same claim, that they will never wish for death because of what their hands have sent forward, is made about the same people in Al-Baqarah.

links.why: the same claim about the same people, in near-identical wording

8.sense: Moves from the wish for death, which the verse before refused, to death as a fact no refusal can hold off. The meeting is stated as certain, then followed by a return to Allah described through the pairing of unseen and witnessed, so that what a person hid and what a person showed both open onto the same account. The verse ends on informing rather than on judgment, keeping the weight on what will be made known.

notes.t: Alim al-ghaybi wash-shahadati, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, is a fixed pairing in the Qur'an that closes off both what a person conceals and what a person displays as grounds for hiding anything from Allah's knowledge.
The same claim, that death reaches a person wherever they are, is made in An-Nisa, adding that it finds a person even inside towers built up high.

links.why: the same claim that death cannot be outrun, with the added image of a fortified tower

9.sense: Gives the surah its name and its single ruling: when the call sounds for the Friday prayer, trade stops and the response is to move toward the remembrance of Allah. Sa'w, the verb for hastening, is read by most exegetes as urgency of intent rather than running, since walking to prayer at a measured pace is what the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have taught elsewhere. The closing clause turns the instruction into a comparison of two goods rather than a bare prohibition, trade against remembrance, and states which one is better.

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ said that when the call to prayer is heard, it should not be met by running, but by walking with calm, praying what is caught and completing what was missed; exegetes cite this to read fas'au here as diligence rather than literal running.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Abu Hurairah

notes.t: Yawm al-jumu'ah names the day by its gathering, from the same root as jama'a, to bring together, rather than by a fixed weekday-name pattern used elsewhere.

Jurists differ on whether the stop on trade binds only the buyer and seller directly party to a transaction at that hour or extends to any commercial activity that would keep a person from reaching the prayer.
notes.src: general fiqh discussion among the schools

links.why: men described elsewhere as those whom neither trade nor commerce divert from the remembrance of Allah

10.sense: Lifts the stop on trade the moment the prayer ends, releasing believers back into the land to seek Allah's bounty in the same breath as commanding His remembrance. Dispersing and seeking are given as permission rather than obligation, set against a remembrance that keeps its plain command and is made frequent. The verse ends on success rather than on reward, tying the sequence back to the same word, fadl, used earlier of the messenger's own sending.

notes.t: Fantashiru stands in the imperative form but is read by classical exegetes as permission following on a prohibition, restoring what verse 9 had set aside rather than commanding dispersal outright; the remembrance command right after it keeps its full imperative force.
Fadl Allah repeats the word used of the messenger's own sending earlier in the surah, so the bounty sought in trade after the prayer is named with the same word as the bounty of guidance itself.
The same phrase, seeking bounty from your Lord, describes trade carried on during the pilgrimage season without blame in Al-Baqarah.

links.why: the same phrase for seeking bounty applied to trade during another act of worship, the pilgrimage
the same command to remember Allah often, addressed to the believers in Al-Ahzab

11.sense: Names the incident behind the surah's closing instruction: a passing caravan and its noise drew people away from the sermon and left the Prophet ﷺ standing to speak to an emptied room. The verse states the loss plainly before answering it, and the answer repeats the same pair, trade and diversion, in reverse order, measured against what is with Allah. It ends by naming Him the best of providers, answering the pull of the caravan's goods with the source those goods came from in the first place.

notes.t: Jabir ibn Abdullah reported that a trade caravan arrived in Madinah while the Prophet ﷺ was giving the Friday sermon, and the people left for it until only twelve men remained with him, at which this verse was revealed.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Jabir ibn Abdullah

notes.t: Qa'iman, "standing", falls at the very end of its clause, holding the image of the Prophet ﷺ left alone mid-sermon to the last word before the answer begins.
Khayru ar-raziqin, best of providers, is used elsewhere as a title for Allah in a prayer for provision, tying the caravan's goods back to their true source.

links.why: the same title, best of providers, used in a prayer asking Allah for provision
a trade named in the surah before this one, offered as the transaction that actually saves and profits
